messages.subject: Estimating Density for multiple species in multiple strata
messages.subject_clean: Estimating Density for multiple species in multiple strata
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I searched the archives and readings relevant to my data and was unable t=
o find an answer.

I have point transect data for many species of birds across 40 different =
strata (8 points in each strata, visited 4 times each in one season).  I =
have followed the protocol in the Alldredge et al 2007 ms for multiple sp=
ecies analysis and have created 6 groups of species based on similarities=
 in detection.  I want to get Density values for each species in each str=
ata, but the only way I can figure to do this is to analyze each group of=
 species (N =3D 6) in each strata individually (N =3D 40).  I then post-s=
tratify by species to get the D estimates (using global detection fxns) a=
nd assess any covariates (using MCDS - observer, time of day, species, et=
c).  This is all well and good except that it would take a VERY LONG time=
 considering that each analysis takes me about 20 minutes...  (40*6*20 =3D=
 80 hours)!  Also, some strata have fewer than 50 detections for some spe=
cies groups (this is an suburban landscape).

I have a feeling that there is an quicker/better way, and would appreciat=
e any feedback.  Possibly conducting the analysis for the species groups =
as a whole and using the parameter estimates from MCDS model to manually =
estimate D for each species in each strata???

Thanks for any help you can provide.  Hopefully I have provided enough in=
formation.

Lesley

messages.subject: Specifying variability in detection function parameters when
messages.subject_clean: Specifying variability in detection function parameters when
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am currently fitting detection functions and calculating design based
population estimates for seabirds counted from boat based line transects
using the mrds package in R.

For cases where sample sizes are too small to allow detection functions to
be fitted I use estimates of the probability of detection from other
studies. To do this I create ddf.ds objects for which the parameter values
and hessian values defining the detection function are provided by the user
rather than fitted. I use the hessian values to control the standard errors
of the parameter estimates. For example, where no error estimates are
available for the probabilities of detection I am using, I use very large
hessian values to implement the (simplifying) assumption of no variability.
In the following snippet of code I fit a detection function (ddf.result1),
and then create a sister model (ddf.result2) which is identical apart from
the fact that I have multiply the hessian value by a factor of 10,
consistent with far greater accuracy in the parameter value estimate (half
normal model with single parameter). With respect to the coefficient of
variation for the Scale coefficient estimate, the Average P estimate and  "N
in covered region" estimate, increasing the hessian value has exactly the
expected effect: it increases the apparent accuracy of estimates. Using dht
to estimate abundance for strata, the same is also true for the standard
errors/cvs for the abundance estimates for each strata: Increasing the
hessian value increases the accuracy of estimates.

However, increasing hessian values is associated with wider confidence
limits: Looking at the dht output for the two models it can be that this is
because although the se estimates for the model with higher hessian values
are lower, the estimates of the degrees of freedom are higher, and the
latter effect outweighs the former.

I've looked at the code within dht.se <http://dht.se> where the degrees of freedom are
calculated, and haven't been able to spot additional variables beyond the
hessian values which need to specified in order to define the variability.
However, I'm  wondering, if I'm missing something, or is it just the
estimate of degrees of freedom is approximate, and this is acceptable error,
given the vast majority of the variability in  abundance estimates resides
in the encounter  rate estimates rather than the detection probability
estimates.

In a nutshell it would hope really usefully to know if my approach of
controlling variability in parameter estimates using hessian values alone is
sound , or is there something else I need to specify.

Hope that makes sense, any help gratefully received.

Best wishes

Nigel Harding

messages.subject: Re: Specifying variability in detection function parameters when
messages.subject_clean: Specifying variability in detection function parameters when
messages.body_plain:
The computation of df is described in Sec 3.6 of Buckland et al Intro to
Distance Sampling. It uses a Saterthwaite approx based on df  and cv for
each component. In your post it isn't clear to me whether you are using
variance of encounter rate and group size from the empirical data and only
inflating the variance for detection probability or what exactly.  I'd
rather see an inflation based on ratio of sample sizes rather than some
number you pick out of the air.  Why not fit a model using all of the
species with species (or species group) as a possible factor variable in
the detection model?

--jeff

messages.body_plain:
Lesley:

You are a little thin on points per stratum to produce convincing=20
measures of precision within each stratum.  Nevertheless, you should be=20
able to streamline your analysis so it does not take as much time as you =

project.

The approach I might take would be largely as you suggest but perhaps=20
using a project template such that a set of models is automatically run=20
for each of your combinations of strata/species group.  That would knock =

down the time per combination I presume (or at least automate it so you=20
can be doing something else).  Is most of the 20 minutes per analysis=20
spent setting up the models, or actually having the computer do the fitti=
ng?

Another approach to producing 240 individual abundance estimates might=20
be via the Distance R package on CRAN, if you are comfortable using the=20
R scripting language.

Feel free to contact me off-list to discuss the niggly details.

messages.body_plain:
Nelli:

The simple answer to your question is that your detection function model
contains as many parameters as you have data points, so there is nothing
remaining to assess model fit.  I can't quite tell from your description
what model you fit to these data (you did not say how many levels each
of your factor covariates possessed), but look through your Distance
output to the section on 'fitted model' where you get to see the number
of parameters estimated by Distance.  I suspect you will see that your
model contains 5 parameters, which is the number of bins of data in the
chi-square table you provided.

Did you have exact distance data, or where they collected in bins? Why
is the lower bound of the first interval 50?

Hope that us useful.

messages.body_plain:
With that number of covariates, you will indeed exceed the number of
bins of data, and your chi-square test will report no remaining degrees
of freedom.

If your colleague's data were collected as exact distances, you would
still have the Kolomogorov-Smirnov or Cramer von Mises tests (which are
insensitive to location of cut points) for goodness of fit testing.
